q7.answer: The email worker, not the API, creates the token. It generates 32 random bytes, writes SHA256(token) and expires_at into the reset row, and emails the link /reset?token=<token> through the provider. The raw token exists only in worker memory and the email, never in Postgres, the queue job or logs.

q8.answer: The API hashes the token from the URL with SHA-256 and selects the reset row WHERE token_hash matches AND used_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now(). A match shows the choose-password form. No match shows the 'link has expired' page. The page-load check is read-only and burns nothing.

q9.answer: There is no separate counter. The count comes from the password_resets table itself: rows for that user with created_at > now() - 1 hour, including burned and expired ones. Old requests drop out because they age past the one-hour window. Rows are kept at least an hour and purged after about 24 hours.

q10.answer: In the request transaction, before the new row is inserted, the API sets used_at on all of the user's unused rows. The burn and the insert commit together, before the job is enqueued. So earlier links die immediately, even if the queue is backed up.

q11.answer: One transaction does four things. It marks the reset row used, updates users.password_hash, burns the user's other unused reset rows and deletes all of the user's sessions rows. The 'password changed' email is enqueued after COMMIT, outside the transaction.

q12.answer: The conditional UPDATE ... SET used_at=now() WHERE token_hash=... AND used_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now() RETURNING user_id is the single gate. Postgres row locking lets only one concurrent submit update the row. The other gets 0 rows, rolls back and sees the expired page.
